extracted.intended_audience: public relations students and practitioners (including government and corporate PR staff)
extracted.subtask_description: Criteria and knowledge standards for public relations practice relating to U.S. law: First Amendment protections and limits, media access, broadcast/cable/internet regulation, FOIA/open-records, commercial vs. political speech, copyright/trademark, libel/privacy, lobbying and campaign-finance rules. Emphasizes what practitioners must know to avoid legal pitfalls and work with legal counsel.

rubrics_metrics.name: Summarize the basic structure of law in the United States
rubrics_metrics.description: Summarize the basic structure of law in the United States.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Know the hierarchy and sources of law: the U.S. Constitution (constitutional law) as final arbiter; statutory law (federal, state, local statutes); administrative law (agency rules and decisions, e.g., FCC, FTC, SEC, NLRB); executive actions; common law (state court rulings derived from English common law); and law of equity. Understanding where a law originates and how it can be superseded helps evaluate its impact on PR practice.

rubrics_metrics.name: Outline major First Amendment principles relevant to PR
rubrics_metrics.description: Outline the major principles of the First Amendment pertaining to freedom of speech and press and explain their relevance to the practice of public relations.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Recognize that First Amendment protects speech and press, informs media relations, and that courts do not recognize a separate category 'public relations speech.' Practitioners should know when to invoke clients' First Amendment rights and when speech may be limited by government regulation.

rubrics_metrics.name: Distinguish commercial speech from political speech
rubrics_metrics.description: Distinguish between commercial and political speech.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Commercial speech concerns buying/selling and must meet two conditions per Virginia State Board of Pharmacy: be about a legal activity and not be misleading. Political speech deals with politics and government; it is highly protected and does not depend on the speaker's identity (First National Bank v. Bellotti). Understand differing levels of constitutional protection and regulatory regimes for each.

rubrics_metrics.name: Describe permissible federal regulation of First Amendment-protected expression in key areas
rubrics_metrics.description: Describe permissible federal regulation of First Amendment–protected expression in election communication, lobbying, communication between labor and management, and financial public relations/investor relations.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Be familiar with campaign finance laws (e.g., Bipartisan Campaign Reform Act/BCRA provisions on soft money, contribution limits, electioneering communications), lobbying disclosure rules (Lobbying Disclosure Act), labor/management communication rules, and SEC/regulatory limits on financial communications.

rubrics_metrics.name: Outline constitutional protection and federal regulation of copyright and trademark
rubrics_metrics.description: Outline constitutional protection and permissible federal regulation of copyright and trademark law.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Know that copyright and trademark law are protected and regulated at federal level; practitioners must be aware of protections and limits when using third-party material in releases, communications, and promotional content. (Chapter lists this as a learning outcome though specifics appear elsewhere in the chapter.)

rubrics_metrics.name: Define and explain libel and privacy law provisions relevant to PR
rubrics_metrics.description: Define and explain the major provisions of libel law and privacy law relevant to public relations work.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Understand elements of defamation (libel), privacy torts, defenses (truth, privilege), and how PR messaging can create liability. (Listed as a learning outcome; practitioner must know to avoid legal pitfalls and coordinate with legal counsel.)

rubrics_metrics.name: Evaluate situations involving legal issues and collaborate with legal staff
rubrics_metrics.description: Public relations practitioners need to know how to evaluate situations involving legal issues if they want to succeed in their jobs.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Practitioners do not practice law, but knowledge of law helps avoid legal pitfalls and facilitates collaboration with an organization's legal staff when required. This includes recognizing when legal counsel should be involved.

rubrics_metrics.name: Understand that media have editorial discretion; no right to compel publication
rubrics_metrics.description: First Amendment protection of press freedom means that no citizen has a guaranteed right to require the print media to publish specific information.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Practitioners should accept journalists' choice whether to use a release or interview a person; court precedent (e.g., striking down a state statute compelling newspapers to give reply space) protects editorial control and means PR cannot force publication.

rubrics_metrics.name: Know broadcast regulation and FCC licensing rationale
rubrics_metrics.description: Broadcast media are subject to government regulation because the airwaves are a scarce public resource; the FCC issues licenses and enforces programming policies under the public interest standard.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Understand that over-the-air broadcasting requires FCC licenses; licensees are trustees for the public. The FCC can regulate technical and content aspects under its authority; the right to use broadcast facilities is not absolute.

rubrics_metrics.name: Recognize cable regulatory differences and use of public access channels
rubrics_metrics.description: Cable operators have more First Amendment rights than broadcasters but less than print; cable regulation (e.g., Cable Communication Policy Act of 1984) led to deregulated rates/program choices and required public, educational, and governmental access channels.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: PR practitioners can use public access channels to reach particular publics directly (e.g., city council meetings). Know cable franchise/regulatory context when planning broadcast/cable campaigns.

rubrics_metrics.name: Treat Internet speech as highly protected but be aware of specific restrictions (e.g., CIPA)
rubrics_metrics.description: Speech on the Internet is fully protected by the First Amendment (Reno v. ACLU), giving PR practitioners broad leeway to send unmediated communication to publics.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use the Internet for direct communication, but be mindful of specific lawful regulations such as CIPA requiring filtering in schools/libraries receiving federal funds; some content restrictions can apply in particular contexts.

rubrics_metrics.name: Be familiar with government access/open-records laws and FOIA limits
rubrics_metrics.description: Outline federal open records and meetings laws; understand the federal Freedom of Information Act (FOIA) applies to executive-branch records and specifies nine exemptions; FOIA covers tangible records, not answers to questions.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Public affairs practitioners must know federal and state open-access laws applicable where they work, respond appropriately to records/meeting requests, and ensure officials understand their obligations. Note that media access rights are no greater than the public's and there is no federal constitutional right to access government-controlled information beyond statutory regimes.

rubrics_metrics.name: Understand corporate expression rights and limits
rubrics_metrics.description: The question of whether organizations have constitutional speech rights is complex: courts have afforded corporations some of the same legal rights as individuals but have also upheld many restrictions.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Recognize corporations/organizations may exercise speech rights (including the right not to speak) but may also be subject to regulations restricting corporate political or commercial communications when the government has a compelling interest.

rubrics_metrics.name: Ensure commercial messages are lawful and not misleading; verify accuracy
rubrics_metrics.description: Commercial speech must be about a legal activity and cannot be misleading.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The FTC regulates advertising truthfulness; public relations practitioners placing or creating advertising or commercial messages have a legal duty to verify accuracy and avoid deceptive practices (illustrated by FTC enforcement actions against misleading 'acai' claims).

rubrics_metrics.name: Know campaign-finance limits and rules on electioneering communications (BCRA basics)
rubrics_metrics.description: Be aware of BCRA (McCain-Feingold) provisions: soft money prohibition, changes to contribution limits, and limits on 'electioneering communications' (ads referring to federal candidates within specified pre-election windows).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Understand who may contribute, limits per donor, disclosure requirements for entities making electioneering communications, and distinctions between national and state party rules. These laws affect PR activity tied to elections or issue advocacy close to elections.

rubrics_metrics.name: Understand lobbying definitions, registration, reporting, and exclusions
rubrics_metrics.description: Know the definitions under lobbying laws (e.g., Lobbying Disclosure Act): a lobbyist makes more than one contact on behalf of a client and spends at least 20% of time over six months on that service; a lobbying contact is communication to covered officials about legislation/rules, grants, permits, programs, or nominations.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Lobbying firms and lobbyists must register and file semiannual reports with names/addresses/financial 'good faith estimates'; lobbying does not include general PR campaigns aimed at public opinion ('grassroots lobbying'), invited testimony before Congress, or ordinary media editorial activity. Nonprofit organizations engaging in lobbying face restrictions (may be prohibited from certain federal grants/contracts). Enforcement has historically been lax, so practitioners should still comply and advise clients accordingly.

rubrics_metrics.name: Public relations in regulated international contexts (example: Brazil)
rubrics_metrics.description: Recognize that law varies internationally; some countries legally regulate PR practice (example: Brazil requires college degree and registration; CONFERP code of ethics makes dissemination of false or misleading information illegal and can strip registration).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When practicing abroad, learn local registration, licensing, and code-of-ethics requirements; noncompliance can result in fines, lawsuits, or loss of right to practice. Codes may include duties to truth, respect human rights, and avoid corrupting communications channels.
